title: Projects a lobbyist raised with the people who then voted
question: When a registered lobbyist reported contacting a voting member about a project’s address, did the project fare differently from like projects, and was it heard with fewer delays?
finding: At the commissions 188 of 873 decisions at an address followed a lobbyist’s reported contact with planning staff or commissioners about that address: 33.5% were changed or disapproved against 26.1% expected for like cases, and where the contact was with a commissioner who then voted (120 decisions) 35.8% against 26.2% (beyond what chance would produce) - changed more often than like cases, not less. Lobbied projects were continued 1.11 times each against 0.52 for the rest; at the Board of Supervisors 64.4% of 59 lobbied appeals were rejected against 79.0% of the other 76 (within what chance would produce, like for like).
how: Lobbyists’ reports to the Ethics Commission give, for each contact, the official, the date, the client, the “issue” and the outcome sought. An address in the issue text (street number and first word of the street name) is matched to the address of a commission item or Board appeal; the contact must fall in the two years before the vote. Commissioners are told apart from planning staff with the same surname by their full names on Form 700 cover pages. “Expected” gives each case the citywide rate for its kind of approval and kind of proposal (or kind of appeal). Continuances per project compare projects whose address appears in any lobbyist contact with planning officials against the rest.
limits: Lobbying is reported. A large or contested project is more likely to hire a lobbyist than a routine one, so a gap in either direction can arise without any favor; the reports do not say which side prevailed. An address match can join two different projects on one lot, and issues described without a street number are missed. Applicants’ names are not in the minutes, so client names cannot be checked against the project. A difference between areas, or between groups of cases, is not proof of bias. Areas differ in what is proposed, in zoning, lot sizes, building ages and land prices, and in who chooses to apply, object or appeal at all.
